glosses: To exceed the allotted time.

examples.text: The previous presentation ran over and ours had to start late.

glosses: To cross by running.

examples.text: The athletes must run over the bridge to reach the finish line.
A further loop siding is passed at Park House, and, just before reaching the power house, the line runs over a 20-ton Avery wagon weighbridge.

glosses: To drive over, causing injury or death.

examples.text: Can you believe somebody would just run over a cat like that?

glosses: To mistreat out of disregard.

examples.text: It is time that all bisexuals and gays that are in prison become unified and stop letting the administration and other inmates run over them.

glosses: To describe briefly; to summarize or recapitulate; to go through or consider quickly.

examples.text: Before we start the project, let's just run over who is doing what.
Each man was running over the what ifs in his mind.

glosses: To rehearse quickly.

examples.text: You'd better run over your statement before going on the platform.

glosses: To overflow.

examples.text: The bath water nearly ran over.

glosses: To score a try.

examples.text: Andrew Bishop then ran over in the closing stages, but it was too late.

glosses: To travel from one end of something to the other.

examples.text: The train went through the tunnel.

glosses: To execute or carry out.
To examine or scrutinize (a number or series of things).

examples.text: Every morning, she went through her mail over a cup of coffee.

After Betty died, Greg and Nicole had the job of going through her apartment and giving things away to charity, no small job since they felt the need to clean everything and make it look as good as possible before giving it away.

glosses: To rob (someone), especially after searching through their clothes.
To enact or recite the entire length of (something).

examples.text: Juve’s indignities in that period also featured a sending-off for Juan Cuadrado, one of their substitutes, and a late goal from Marco Asensio when the thousands of Madridistas were already going through their victory songs.

glosses: To undergo, suffer, experience.

examples.text: I went through a lengthy immigration process before I was allowed across the border.
She's yet to go through puberty, although she's already 17.
I feel certain that I am going mad again. I feel we cant[sic] go through another of those terrible times. And I shant[sic] recover this time.

glosses: To use up or wear out (clothing etc.).

examples.text: Her family drinks so much milk that they go through two gallons a week.
I've gone through two pairs of shoes already this holiday.

glosses: To progress to the next stage of something.

examples.text: If United don't lose by more than 2 goals, they should go through to the next round.

glosses: To reach an intended destination after passing through some process.

examples.text: My payment hasn't gone through yet.
I don't think my instant messages are going through.

And you have to be careful. If you don't book your parking in double-quick time, you risk a fine, so always double-check that your payment has gone through. Some operators don't even send you an email or text to say you've paid.

glosses: To beat, fight or attack (someone).
To be present and intense.

examples.text: The cardamom goes through the cake.

glosses: To go past something; to go too far.

examples.text: When you drive, you must remember to not overshoot the parking space and end up with two wheels over the line.

As a result of the accident at Southend Airport when a Hermes aircraft overshot the runway and fouled the down Shenfield to Southend Victoria line between Rochford and Prittlewell, the Eastern Region is considering warning arrangements, which have already been provided on some lines running past aerodromes.

A ScotRail Driver: […] A good friend of mine overshot two stations back-to-back a couple of years ago. He tried to stop at one station and slid by it. Tried to stop at the next station. He slid by that, too.

glosses: To shoot beyond; to shoot too far to hit something.

examples.text: not to overshoot his game

glosses: To pass swiftly over; to fly beyond.
To exceed.

examples.text: to overshoot the truth

That fire abated that impells rash youth,

Measured this way humanity was last at sustainable levels in the 1980s. Now it has overshot by some 20 percent.
The amount a letter overshoots is based on the design, but your eye shouldn’t notice it.

glosses: To venture too far; to overreach (oneself).
To record too much photographic footage.
The amount by which something goes too far.

examples.text: Let's see if we can predict and correct for the overshoot.

glosses: The situation where the population of a species exceeds its environment's carrying capacity.

examples.text: With appropriate choice and action such uncontrolled decline could be avoided; overshoot could instead be resolved by a conscious effort to reduce humanity's demand on the planet.
Population overshoot is therefore unlikely to yield to management. Rather, the usual suspects will enter the scene and do their thing: starvation, disease, […] violence […] [and] death […].
Our core ecological problem is not climate change. It is overshoot, of which global warming is a symptom.

glosses: The portion of a letter extending above the capline of other letters of the same font, or the relative degree of such extent.

examples.text: The portion resting beyond the capline or baseline is called overshoot.
The bowl of the D and the O are usually not identical, as most D forms do not have overshoot or undershoot.

glosses: Aplatir, briser quelque chose par un grand poids, par une forte compression, par un coup violent.

examples.text: C’est là, sans aucun doute, que près de cinquante navires anglais, danois et hollandais furent écrasés par les glaces en 1777.
Le canot bascule sur le berthon, se met à glisser vers l'avant écrasant une trentaine de personnes et blessant grièvement à la jambe Isaac Lehmann.
Bruno, épargne-moi ton baratin de Rock Machine. T’as de la misère à écraser une araignée.
Écraser des groseilles, du verjus.

glosses: Heurter violemment et accidentellement.

examples.text: Tout le monde levait la tête vers le ciel. En ce seul jour, le nombre des gens écrasés dans la rue fut plus élevé qu’au cours des trois derniers mois.

[…] qu'avant les grandes bandes blanches qui permettent de traverser les rues en toute quiétude ou de se faire écraser dans son droit, il y avait de jolis clous argentés qui délimitaient les passages pour piétons.

glosses: Surcharger.

examples.text: Cet homme est écrasé sous le poids des affaires.
Ce travail m’écrase.
Cette responsabilité m’écrase.
Je suis écrasé de demandes.

glosses: Perdre quelqu’un ; détruire entièrement ses moyens de fortune, de considération, anéantir, réduire à rien.

examples.text: Les Magyars ne surent même pas défendre les Slovaques contre l’invasion étrangère. En 1244, ils furent écrasés par mes Mongols qui se répandirent sur le pays.
Enfin la gendarmerie se botte à tout propos pour eux… ils vous écraseront…

glosses: Se montrer plus fort, plus habile ; prendre un grand avantage sur quelqu’un.

examples.text: Écraser quelqu’un dans une discussion, dans un débat.

glosses: Enregistrer un contenu dans un fichier ou document en supprimant le contenu antérieur.

examples.text: Tu as écrasé ce fichier ‽ Et comment je fais, moi, maintenant, pour voir ce que tu as supprimé ?

glosses: Se taire.

examples.text: Il a raison, alors j’écrase.

glosses: Dormir profondément, ce qui écrase le support du fait de l'absence de tonus musculaire pendant le sommeil

examples.text: Les chiens, quand ils ont couru toute la journée dans la forêt, qu'est-ce qu'ils écrasent !

glosses: Venir heurter violemment la surface d’un objet plus rigide et plus large, au point de se déformer.

examples.text: Il pleuvait. Par instants, on entendait l’averse s’écraser contre la verrière du haut. — (Francis Carco, L’Homme de minuit, Éditions Albin Michel, Paris, 1938)

Au milieu de toutes ces impressions, un espoir subsistait : il finirait fatalement par descendre quelque part, et alors, s’il ne s’écrasait pas dans la dégringolade, quelqu’un ou quelque société peut-être le réexpédierait, lui et le ballon, en Angleterre.
Cependant, au milieu de la chaussée, des nègres se poursuivaient à coup de boules de neige et parfois, une de ces boules, manquant son but, s'écrasait contre une devanture.

examples.text: Местами только переезжали с мыса на мыс, водою на лодках…
Не день, не два уже он переезжает горы.
Подъехал к тому месту, где сутки назад переезжал по льду; вышедшая из берегов речка гнала по раздвинувшемуся руслу грязные воды, легко кружила на середине отрезок плетня и половинку колесного обода.
Троллейбус седьмого маршрута переезжал через рельсы на пересечении проспектов Ленина и Строителей, в этот момент ему в бок врезался трамвай номер 1.

glosses: неперех. уехав откуда-либо, перебираться на другое, новое место; менять место своего пребывания

examples.text: Я веду совершенно кочующую жизнь, переезжая из шалаша в шалаш, от огня к огню.
Ты знаешь, милая Полина, что петербургский обычай повелевает каждому порядочному семейству переезжать на дачу.
Он ведь тоже любит часто переезжать с квартиры на квартиру и недоплачивать.
Любит на готовое приехать. Переезжай, говорит, Авдей, а я ужо к вечеру буду, да и был таков.
Он послезавтра переезжает в нашу деревеньку и будет жить со мной на одной квартире.

glosses: перен., разг., шутл. или ирон. менять что-либо привычное, устоявшееся на новое

examples.text: Кроме того, абсолютное большинство российских пользователей Mac «переезжает» на новую платформу с привычной Windows.
